subject: geography

moments.title: Longitude Act
moments.body: After the 1707 Scilly naval disaster (around 2,000 sailors lost when warships ran aground partly through navigation error), Parliament offers £20,000 (around £3 million today) for a method to determine longitude at sea to within half a degree.
moments.takeaway: Latitude can be found by the noon altitude of the sun. Longitude requires either accurate astronomy (the lunar-distance method) or accurate time.

moments.title: Harrison's H4 chronometer
moments.who: John Harrison, Yorkshire carpenter and clockmaker
moments.body: Harrison completes H4, a watch around 13 cm across. Tested on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761-62, it lost only 5 seconds in 81 days. The Board of Longitude paid Harrison in instalments only after political battles; Parliament finally awarded him the balance in 1773 — aged 80.

quote.text: I think I may make bold to say that there is neither any other Mechanical or Mathematical thing in the World that is more beautiful or curious in texture than this my watch.

moments.takeaway: Harrison's chronometers transformed maritime navigation. By 1800 a chronometer was standard on Royal Navy ships.

moments.title: Cook's three Pacific voyages
moments.who: James Cook and the Endeavour, Resolution, Discovery
moments.body: Cook's voyages mapped New Zealand (1769-70), the east coast of Australia (1770), much of the Pacific, and crossed the Antarctic Circle. He carried a Kendall copy of Harrison's H4 on his second voyage and praised it.
moments.takeaway: Accurate longitude meant accurate maps. Cook's charts of New Zealand were used into the 20th century.

now.title: Navigation reshaped
now.body: Modern GPS provides position to a few metres anywhere on Earth. The fundamental challenge — knowing where you are in the absence of landmarks — is the same problem Harrison and Cook faced. Dava Sobel's 'Longitude' (1995) made the story famous; the Royal Observatory Greenwich displays H1-H4. The International Meridian Conference (Washington, 1884) made Greenwich the global zero.
now.open_questions: Cook's voyages opened the Pacific to European contact, with profound consequences for indigenous societies — Hawaiians (where Cook died in 1779), Maori, Aboriginal Australians. The legacy is now read with very different politics than in Cook's day.

reflection: A technical problem (longitude) drove a scientific revolution (chronometry) that enabled European empire-making in the Pacific. Geography's history is inseparable from the politics of exploration.
